title: Panel-measured economic insecurity predicted participation and right-leaning presidential preference
source_unit: Understanding America Study panel respondents with repeated household-income observations and 2016 presidential preference reports

observations.period: UAS income observations from May 2014 to November 2016; 2016 U.S. presidential election poll

denominator.unit: UAS respondents ages 18–65, not retired, with at least five household-income observations and participation in the Election Poll Study

economic_insecurity_and_vote_probability.value: greater economic insecurity predicted a higher probability of voting in the presidential election
economic_insecurity_and_vote_probability.unit: reported probability of voting; observational panel association

economic_insecurity_and_trump_probabilit.value: greater economic insecurity predicted greater support for Donald Trump
economic_insecurity_and_trump_probabilit.unit: reported candidate-vote probability; observational panel association

economic_insecurity_and_clinton_probabil.value: greater economic insecurity predicted lower support for Hillary Clinton
economic_insecurity_and_clinton_probabil.unit: reported candidate-vote probability; observational panel association

observations.method: Constructed individual economic-insecurity measures from the time profile of repeated banded household income in the UAS, then related the last five pre-election income observations to reported probabilities of voting and candidate choice while conditioning on current resources and demographic/labor-market covariates.
observations.uncertainty: This is an observational panel association, not a randomized shock or causal estimate. The insecurity index depends on modeled income-band values, observation timing, discounting, and sample retention; candidate and turnout outcomes are reported probabilities rather than validated ballots.
observations.subgroup: UAS adults ages 18–65, not retired, with sufficient income-history observations; the UAS panel is described as representative of the United States, but the analytic restrictions reduce the source population.
observations.counterinterpretation: Economic insecurity may mobilize or polarize through perceived risk, identity, partisan attribution, or concern about future resources rather than through reduced material capacity; the positive participation association contrasts with hardship-to-withdrawal results from other designs.

related_sources.claim: Published Oxford Economic Papers article identifier
Author-hosted published-version PDF used to inspect UAS design and sample construction

boundary: This record adds a panel-measured economic-insecurity-to-political-preference contrast: insecurity predicted greater reported voting probability and Trump support in the 2016 U.S. presidential context, conditional on current resources. It does not establish causality, generalized distrust, ballot-validated turnout, or a universal hardship-to-mobilization mechanism.
